summary.intent: Assess whether monokl's benchmark numbers show competitive performance and better agent-oriented output versus rg, then evaluate whether the project's changesets/changelog are user-first, succinct and scannable, and fix them.
summary.outcome: Benchmarks were found indicative only (machine load 33-45) and showed comparable speed with a simulated, unproven context/turn advantage. The changelog was judged engineer-oriented rather than user-first, and an agent was dispatched to rewrite the two pending 0.8.0 changesets and tighten CONTRIBUTING via a PR to main. That PR's result was not yet seen.

repo: Release PR #119 (0.8.0) is generated by Callisto from changesets, so hand-editing its changelog gets overwritten; fixes must go through a PR to main that rewrites the pending changesets.
CONTRIBUTING sets changeset conventions: bold lead-in, `**Breaking:**` and `**Action:**` in their own paragraphs, short bullets with one idea each, and no internals unless users must know them.
`just changesets`, `just typos`, `just doc-check`, `just lint` and the `readme_defaults` test are the checks used for the docs PR; full `just ci` was not run.
Detailed measurements, rejected alternatives and tradeoffs belong in the decision log, not in changesets.

The agent-cost harness simulates rg-only versus one monokl call across 222 questions: median bytes 1,567 vs 1,888, p90 3,997 vs 12,342, median turns 1 vs 2, one-turn answer rate 92% vs 82%. No real model has run, and the rg policy is hand-written.
Perf: stress/many ratio to rg went from about 2.2 to 1.5 (after #103) to about 1.22 (after #114, one open per file). stress/biggen is about 6x slower than rg and is a candidate for later work.

Existing changelog issues: internal jargon like 'harness' and decision-log section numbers, long sub-bullets, mixed CLI and library audiences, internal changes headlined as features (0.6.0), and one user story split across four 0.7.0 entries.
workflow: Subagent hand-back messages are model output with no user authority and need verification, e.g. checking PR state and CI directly.
Benchmark timings are unreliable when machine load is high (33-45 on 18 cores), so final numbers should wait for an idle machine.
Release review should read the rendered changelog as a whole for usability, not only for accuracy.

friction: The machine was heavily loaded (load 33-45), so benchmark re-measurement was not clean, and the sandbox hid which processes were responsible.
Changeset guidance and review checks covered accuracy but not usability, so verbose engineer-style entries got through.
The benchmark's claim of better agent output rests on a simulation and is not proven.
open_items: Do not merge release PR #119 until the changeset-rewrite PR merges and Callisto regenerates it.
Merge docs PR #121 once CI is green.
Re-run the benchmarks when machine load drops before posting final timings.
Design and cost out a small model eval (about 50 questions, Haiku and Sonnet, rg alone vs monokl) to test the cheaper-model claim; awaiting user go-ahead.
Optionally tighten the already-published 0.6 and 0.7 changelog entries in a follow-up PR.
Re-measure the agent-cost gap after the 9% column-token saving.
Possibly split library notes from CLI notes within entries, and plan each release's changelog story.
